title: Saving rainwater for the garden
description: A simple water butt catches roof rain that plants prefer, and spares treated tap water for the jobs that need it.

body.heading: Why rainwater suits plants
paragraphs: Tap water is treated to be safe to drink, which is more processing than a tomato plant requires. Rainwater is soft, untreated and at outdoor temperature, and many plants, especially acid-loving ones like blueberries and camellias, genuinely prefer it.
Collecting it also slows the rush of storm water into drains during heavy rain, a small but real help in places troubled by flooding.

body.heading: Setting up a water butt
paragraphs: A water butt connects to a downpipe from the roof with a simple diverter kit, filling when it rains and stopping automatically when full. Even a modest butt holds enough to water pots and new plants through a dry week or two.
Stand it on bricks or a purpose-made stand so a watering can fits under the tap, and keep the lid on: it keeps out leaves, insects and curious wildlife, and stops mosquitoes breeding in still water.

body.heading: Using what you catch
paragraphs: Water at the base of plants in the morning or evening, when less is lost to evaporation, and aim the water at roots rather than leaves. A full can used slowly beats a quick splash that runs off the surface.
In winter, an empty or partially drained butt avoids freeze damage in cold snaps. Like most garden habits, rainwater saving is seasonal, simple and quietly satisfying once it becomes routine.

takeaway: Catch the roof's rain in a butt, keep the lid on, and water roots in the cool of the day.
